title: Find the biggest shift
concept: How do you compare two distributions?
summary: Input drift shows up as a change in how traffic spreads across buckets, not as a change in raw counts. Comparing shares rather than counts keeps a busy day from looking like a shift, and the largest single move is what an operator investigates first.
example: A bucket holding 30% of baseline traffic and 45% of live traffic has moved 15 percentage points.
takeaway: Compare shares rather than counts, and round before comparing so two near-equal moves do not swap places on floating-point noise.
instruction: Given baseline and live objects mapping bucket name to a nonnegative count, return {bucket, gap, drifted}. For every bucket appearing in either input, treating a missing bucket as 0, take the absolute difference in share expressed in percentage points and round it to two decimal places. Return the largest rounded gap and the bucket where it occurs, breaking ties by the smaller bucket name. drifted is true when gap is at least 10. Return {bucket: null, gap: 0, drifted: false} when either side has no observations.
hint: Turn counts into shares, round each bucket's gap before comparing, and break ties by name so near-equal moves stay deterministic.
